Driver Behavior Profiling from Telematics

Can we recognise driving behaviors — safe, aggressive, distracted — from raw sensor data alone, without ever seeing a label? This notebook finds out, using PCA to compress the sensor streams and K-Means to discover the groups.

1. The Dataset

It was synthetically generated, taken from kaggle vehicle telemetry for driver behavior. Originally the dataset has a target label, but we are going to remove it and explore the data without those labels. The idea is to see if we can identify and classify drivers behaviors based on their telemetry data.

Code 
import pandas as pd
df_telematics = pd.read_csv('data/Driver_Behavior.csv')
df_telematics_analysis = df_telematics.drop(columns=['behavior_label'])

2. Correlation Structure

Before compressing anything, we look at how the sensors relate to each other — the correlation blocks below are exactly what PCA will exploit.

Code 
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
corr = df_telematics_analysis[[
    "throttle",
    "brake_pressure",
    "accel_x",
    "speed_kmph",
    "accel_y",
    "steering_angle",
    "headway_distance",
    "lane_deviation",
    "reaction_time",
    "phone_usage",

]].corr()

sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm', fmt=".2f")
plt.title("Correlation Matrix")
plt.show()

The steering_angle is truly independent, all correlations are very close to \(0\).

Correlation between phone_usage and reaction_time is very high at \(0.91\), suggest that the if the driver is on their phone, their reaction time will be slow, and if the reaction time is slow, it’s very likely that the driver was on their phone.

Code 
aggression_vars = [
    'throttle',
    'brake_pressure',
    'accel_x',
    'speed_kmph',
    'accel_y',
]

aggression_corr = df_telematics[aggression_vars].corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
sns.heatmap(
    aggression_corr,
    annot=True,
    cmap='Reds',
    fmt=".2f",
    linewidths=0.5
)
plt.title("Correlation: The Aggression Box")
plt.show()

Looking at the correlation of accel_x, brake_pressure and throttle we can infer that aggressive drivers press the gas and jump straight to smashing the brake pedal without “coasting.” This seems like a classic signature of “tailgating,” or speeding up to something, then panic braking.

The speed_kmph has a lower correlation, indicating that the aggression behavior is more about force, because probably we can find aggresive behavior not at high speeds.

The difference on the correlation values between accel_x and accel_y with the other variables, tell us that the aggresive behavior is likely to happen in a straight line reckless driving rather than a drift king cornering behavior.

3. Dimensionality Reduction (PCA)

We standardize the features and let PCA find the directions of maximum variance. The scree plot tells us how many components are worth keeping.

Code 
from statsmodels.multivariate.pca import PCA

pca_sm = PCA(df_telematics_analysis, standardize=True)
Code 
pca_sm.plot_scree(log_scale=False)
plt.title("Elbow Method for PCA")
plt.show()
print(pca_sm.rsquare[pca_sm.rsquare < 0.9])
ncomp
0    0.000000
1    0.427785
2    0.703020
3    0.803028
4    0.851606
5    0.893346
Name: rsquare, dtype: float64

The elbow method suggests two components explain 70% of the variance, and three components explain 80%.

I think that three components are more adequate.

Code 
pca_3 = PCA(df_telematics_analysis, standardize=True, ncomp=3)
Code 
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.heatmap(pca_3.loadings, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm', center=0)
plt.title("What does each component represent?")
plt.ylabel("Original Features")
plt.xlabel("Principal Components")
plt.show()

with three components we can see a separation between those three. ### PC1 — aggression highs: - throttle - brake_pressure - accel_x lows: - headway_distance ### PC2 — distraction highs: - lane_deviation - phone_usage - reaction_time ### PC3 — steering geometry lows: - steering_angle

Why does the PC3 have the lowest steering_angle value?

Code 
pca_3_values = pca_3.factors.iloc[:, 2]
plt.scatter(df_telematics_analysis['steering_angle'], pca_3_values, alpha=0.6, color='blue')
plt.xlabel('steering_angle')
plt.ylabel('PC3')
plt.title('PCA of steering_angle vs PC3')
plt.show()

The fact that we have a perfect line in the relationship between the steering_angle and the PC3, means that this is the only behavior that can be grouped on this component.

We assume that steering doesn’t define anything on the other two Principal Components, it could not be grouped on those components.

4. Reading the Projection

Right side — high aggression, low distraction

that represents the Aggressive drivers, they have higher values on the PC1. ### Top left — high distraction, low aggression that represents the distracted drivers, they have higher values on the PC2. ### Bottom left — the safe drivers the Safe-Chill behavior, where they don’t have any high value on the PC1 or PC2 components.

Code 
importance = (pca_3.loadings ** 2).sum(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
importance.plot(kind='bar', color='teal')
plt.title("Which Sensors Drive the Most Variance?")
plt.ylabel("Importance Score (Sum of Squared Loadings)")
plt.show()

5. If You Could Only Afford Two Sensors

if we can afford only 2 sensors for detecting distracted behavior, we should choose phone_usage and reaction_time. if we repeat the same exercise for detecting aggressive behavior, we should choose brake_pressure and throttle.

6. A Reusable Prediction Pipeline

We package the whole approach — scaling, PCA, K-Means — into a single scikit-learn pipeline that can label new telematics data end to end.

To validate inductive generalization and prevent data leakage, we split the data into an 80% training set (to fit the scaler, PCA, and cluster centroids) and a 20% test set (simulating unseen incoming telematics streams).

Code 
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

seed = 42

X = df_telematics.drop(columns=['behavior_label'])
y = df_telematics['behavior_label']

# 80/20 train/test split to evaluate out-of-sample generalization
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=seed, stratify=y
)

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler()),
    ('pca', PCA(n_components=3)),
    ('clusterer', KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=seed))
])

pipeline.fit(X_train)
y_train_clusters = pipeline.predict(X_train)
y_test_clusters = pipeline.predict(X_test)
Code 
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, homogeneity_score

train_ari = adjusted_rand_score(y_train, y_train_clusters)
test_ari = adjusted_rand_score(y_test, y_test_clusters)
train_homo = homogeneity_score(y_train, y_train_clusters)
test_homo = homogeneity_score(y_test, y_test_clusters)

print(f"Train Adjusted Rand Score: {train_ari:.4f} (~{train_ari:.2f})")
print(f"Test Adjusted Rand Score:  {test_ari:.4f} (~{test_ari:.2f})")
print(f"Train Homogeneity Score:   {train_homo:.4f}")
print(f"Test Homogeneity Score:    {test_homo:.4f}")
Train Adjusted Rand Score: 0.9997 (~1.00)
Test Adjusted Rand Score:  0.9990 (~1.00)
Train Homogeneity Score:   0.9992
Test Homogeneity Score:    0.9976

We achieved an Adjusted Rand Score of \(0.9997\) on the training set and \(0.9990\) on the withheld test set (both rounding to \(1.00\)). This indicates a near-perfect alignment between our unsupervised clusters and the ground truth on both training and test data.

It confirms that the driver behaviors (Safe, Aggressive and Distracted) are linearly separable in the PCA space, and our pipeline can autonomously identify these profiles on new, unseen telematics records without retraining.

A near-perfect score deserves a caveat: this dataset is synthetic, and its generator produced cleanly separable behaviors. Real telematics data is far noisier and would not cluster this cleanly; what the test score validates is the pipeline’s generalization and deployment logic, not immediate production-readiness.

Code 
confusion_df = pd.crosstab(
    y_test,
    y_test_clusters,
    rownames=['Actual Label (Test Set)'],
    colnames=['Pipeline Cluster']
)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(confusion_df, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues')
plt.title("Mapping Unsupervised Clusters to True Labels (Test Set)")
plt.show()

7. Conclusions

  1. The behaviors are real, structured signal. Three principal components — aggression, distraction, and steering geometry — explain ~80% of the variance in the raw sensor streams.
  2. Unsupervised methods recover the ground truth. K-Means on the PCA space matches the withheld labels out of sample (~0.999 test ARI) on this synthetic dataset.
  3. Sensor budgets can be optimized. If hardware is constrained, phone_usage + reaction_time capture distraction, and brake_pressure + throttle capture aggression.
  4. The pipeline is deployable. The scaling → PCA → K-Means pipeline labels new data end to end and would serve as a solid baseline for real, noisier telematics — where the next steps are robustness checks, cluster-stability analysis, and drift monitoring.
